title: Qualifying R&D activities for breweries and distilleries
description: Breweries and distilleries can claim the federal R&D credit under IRC Section 41 for novel formulations, fermentation trials and process optimization.
summary: U.S. breweries, cideries, and distilleries can claim the federal R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41 for qualifying activities such as novel formulation and fermentation trials, process optimization, and packaging engineering. Each project must pass the Four-Part Test, and only qualified wages, supplies, computer rental, and contract research count as QREs; general overhead and standard utilities are excluded.

body.text: U.S. breweries, cideries, and distilleries can claim the federal R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41 for qualifying activities such as novel formulation and fermentation trials, process optimization, and packaging engineering. Each project must pass the Four-Part Test, and only qualified wages, supplies, computer rental, and contract research count as QREs; general overhead and standard utilities are excluded.

Breweries, cideries, and distilleries operating in the United States conduct extensive biochemical, microbiological, and process-engineering experimentation that qualifies for the federal Research and Development (R&D) Tax Credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41). Because commercial fermentation and spirit production depend on manipulating living biological systems, enzymatic conversions, volatile congener and ester kinetics, colloidal stability, and low-oxygen packaging engineering, non-routine technical trials across the production value chain frequently satisfy the statutory Four-Part Test for qualified research. When properly substantiated, the credit delivers a permanent, dollar-for-dollar reduction in federal income tax liability—or up to $500,000 annually in payroll tax offsets for qualified small businesses under current IRS Form 6765 Section D instructions (increased from the historical $250,000 cap under the 2015 PATH Act through the Inflation Reduction Act)—accompanied by a 1-year carryback and a 20-year carryforward for unused credits under 26 U.S.C. § 39(a)(1). Furthermore, following the enactment of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, signed July 4, 2025), domestic research and experimental (R&E) expenditures incurred in tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, are once again 100% immediately deductible under newly enacted 26 U.S.C. § 174A (with transition guidance issued in IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-28), eliminating the mandatory 5-year domestic capitalization regime that applied from 2022 through 2024.

Capturing and defending these tax incentives under Internal Revenue Service (IRS) examination requires bridging a persistent divide between fermentation science and tax accounting. Generalist tax preparers routinely evaluate brewery and distillery operations solely through general ledger accounts, categorizing experimental pilot batches, failed fermentations, and process-optimization trials as standard Cost of Goods Sold (COGS). Conversely, specialized R&D tax advisors trained in biochemistry, microbiology, and chemical engineering can translate empirical production records—such as Headspace Gas Chromatography (HS-GC) ester profiles, European Brewing Convention (EBC) turbidity logs, dissolved oxygen (DO) measurements, and congener assays—into the project-level technical narratives required by Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(d) and the mandatory Section G business-component reporting rules on IRS Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) taking effect for tax years beginning in 2026.

items: Exclusion of Overheads and Standard Utilities under U.S. IRC § 41: Removing ineligible overheads and standard utilities revises the dashboard's hypothetical specialist QRE total per $1 million of production cost from $135,000 to $110,000 (and the generalist baseline from $55,000 to $50,000), yielding an IRC § 41-compliant QRE uplift of +120.00% (a 2.20x multiple), rather than the dashboard's unadjusted +145.45% (a 2.45x multiple, misstated in the dashboard's toggle text as "3x").

body.text: Core Qualifying R&D Domains in Brewing, Cidermaking, and Distilling

Qualifying research in fermentation and distillation spans the entire technical lifecycle of beverage production, from raw substrate selection and mash conversion to yeast kinetics, distillation or filtration, and packaging engineering. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d), these activities qualify when they are undertaken to resolve measurable technical uncertainties through systematic experimentation grounded in biological, physical, or engineering sciences.
Novel Formulation, Fermentable Substrates, and Flavor Chemistry

Formulation R&D in breweries, cideries, and distilleries goes beyond routine culinary recipe adjustments; it involves manipulating complex biochemical substrates and microbial agents whose interactions cannot be predicted in advance. Qualifying product development begins with testing unconventional ingredients and substrate hybrids, including locally sourced fruit blends, specific cider apple varietals, experimental hop cultivars, supportive protease preparations, and alternative cereal mash compositions, as well as developing hybrid fermentation styles such as co-fermenting cider must with malted barley wort or aging spirits and beers in trial wood barrels. In parallel, brewers and distillers investigate alternative yeast strains and mixed-culture fermentations—such as non-standard Saccharomyces strains, wild yeasts like Brettanomyces (which metabolize long-chain carbohydrates in specialty and Belgian lambic fermentations to generate distinctive spicy, smoky, and barnyard aromas), lactic or acetic acid bacteria, and distinct distillery yeast strains that alter alcoholic fermentation efficiency and the concentration of selected volatile congeners in distilled spirits.

Formulating specialized functional beverages that must satisfy strict analytical constraints—such as reduced-alcohol beers, certified organic ferments, or gluten-free beers—introduces acute biochemical uncertainty regarding yeast nutrient deprivation, foam stability, mouthfeel, and flavor stability. In gluten-free beer development, as documented in technical literature from AEB Group, brewers conduct enzymatic trials using Bacillus subtilis-derived endoproteases (such as Endozym Protease GF) to hydrolyze peptide linkages in proline-rich proteins, testing enzyme dosages (in g/hL of cold wort) to achieve partial or total gluten degradation (measured in mg/L via Competitive ELISA) while verifying via Nibem testing that foam stability is preserved.
Process Optimization, Fermentation Kinetics, and Smart Industrial Engineering

A second major category of qualifying R&D targets process efficiency, batch-to-batch consistency, and commercial scale-up from pilot systems (such as 5-barrel or 10-barrel pilot units) to full production capacity. Modifying established biological or chemical production systems introduces multi-variable engineering and biochemical uncertainties.

Upstream process R&D frequently begins with raw material specification refinement and mash regime optimization. In malting and mashing research, brewers and distillers must manage raw barley moisture (which must remain at or below 12% to prevent mold growth and the accumulation of the Fusarium mycotoxin deoxynivalenol, or DON, requiring independent laboratory testing of both raw barley and finished malt) and maintain two-row malting barley nitrogen below 2.0% (11.0%–13.0% protein) with over 90% kernel plumpness. Excessive protein reduces starch extract and creates haze, whereas insufficient protein deprives yeast of Free Amino Nitrogen (FAN) and limits diastatic enzyme synthesis. During mashing and spirit substrate preparation, technical teams experiment with enzymatic hydrolysis strategies—such as comparing single-infusion mashing (held at 65.5°C per Institute of Brewing and Distilling [IoB] protocols) against step-mash Congress regimes (ramping from 45°C to 70°C per European Brewing Convention [EBC] and American Society of Brewing Chemists [ASBC] standards) or Separate Hydrolysis and Fermentation (SHF) in spirit mashes—alongside water chemistry adjustments (targeting a mash-in pH of 5.2 and calcium ion concentrations of 70–80 mg/L in the mash to precipitate oxalates and at least 100 mg/L in the kettle boil to promote protein coagulation into trub).

Downstream process optimization includes establishing new production specifications—specifically refining mixing times, batching sequences, and cooking temperatures—to reduce waste, control viscosity, Brix, pH, and titratable acidity, or comply with federal, state, and local health regulations.

At the industrial scale, process engineering R&D increasingly integrates Internet of Things (IoT) sensor networks, cloud telemetry, and artificial intelligence (AI) for resource optimization and decarbonization. Subsequent February 2026 corporate disclosures from Heineken report that the Connected Brewery program scaled in 2025 to over 1,200 deployments—reaching nearly 100 Smart Breweries (connecting roughly 900 production lines and 7,000 machines via in-house IoT kits and seven AI-driven modules optimizing wort kettles, wort coolers, pasteurizers, bottle washers, and cooling plants) and over 150 Connected Worker sites (integrating over 80% of operators and introducing "CoBrain," a multilingual generative AI diagnostic tool), generating over €18 million in annual savings and reducing wort kettle evaporation rates from 4.5% down to 3.0% at trial facilities such as Ponta Grossa. For tax compliance purposes, a specialist distinguishes the routine purchase of off-the-shelf machinery from the qualified engineering R&D required to design custom sensor architectures, calibrate closed-loop process control software, and validate thermodynamic efficiency parameters at industrial scale.
Packaging Engineering, Dissolved Oxygen Mitigation, and Container Compatibility

The third core domain of brewing and beverage R&D addresses post-fermentation physical, chemical, and microbiological stability through packaging line engineering and materials science. The primary engineering challenge during canning, bottling, and kegging is preventing oxygen ingress. Even trace quantities of dissolved oxygen (DO) or headspace oxygen trigger rapid oxidative degradation: peer-reviewed brewing analyses and packaging engineering reports note that lipid oxidation generates trans-2-nonenal (imparting a wet-cardboard off-flavor detectable at just 0.03 ppm, or 30 ppb, of Total Package Oxygen [TPO]), Strecker degradation of amino acids creates sherry-like aldehydes in malt-rich beers, and oxidation at 0.1 ppm DO degrades roughly 33% of volatile hop terpenes and iso-alpha-acids within 30 days (with 0.5–2.0 ppm headspace oxygen breaking down roughly 40% of hop compounds in IPAs within a month).

As packaging equipment manufacturer Wild Goose Filling emphasizes, 1 liter of ambient air dissolved into a 3,000-liter bright beer tank raises DO by 100 ppb, meaning inline filling equipment cannot guarantee sub-threshold DO performance without site-specific process engineering. According to technical benchmarks reported by packaging machinery vendors XMalan Filler and Levapack, breweries and cideries conduct systematic packaging line trials—testing subsurface bottom-actuated fill heads, multi-stage flow-rate restriction, 2°C process cooling (which reduces oxygen solubility by 40%), counter-pressure CO2 equalization (12–15 PSI), pre-fill nitrogen purging (where a 2024 canning line trial optimizing purge cycles from 8 seconds to 5 seconds cut oxygen ingress by 32% and kept residual headspace oxygen below 0.5%), CO2 underlid gassing, foam-pulse control, and vacuum-assisted crown sealing (shrinking air gaps from ~0.8 mm to under 0.1 mm)—to drive DO pickup below 20–50 ppb. Related packaging R&D includes prototyping small-batch kegs, crowlers, and eco-friendly (biodegradable, compostable, or recyclable) materials.

Aluminum beverage cans are coated internally with thin polymeric liners—traditionally bisphenol A (BPA) epoxy, BPA-non-intent (BPA-NI) epoxy, or acrylic resins—to prevent direct contact between the beverage and bare 3004-alloy aluminum. While standard beers (pH 4.0–5.0, titratable acidity <200 mg/L) exhibit minimal corrosion (0.04–0.33 mg/L dissolved aluminum), sour beers and acidic fermented beverages possess low pH (3.0–3.9) and elevated organic acid loads, primarily lactic acid (1.9–8.9 g/L) and acetic acid (0.3–1.4 g/L). Peer-reviewed research by Sheehan, Montgomery, Goddard, and Sacks (2024) in the Journal of the American Society of Brewing Chemists demonstrates that undissociated (neutral) lactic and acetic acid molecules permeate microscopic pores in polymeric can liners far more aggressively than inorganic phosphoric acid (producing 2.54 mg/L vs. 0.47 mg/L dissolved aluminum in equinormal model tests), oxidizing the underlying aluminum metal via the electrochemical reaction:
2 Al(s) + 6 H+(aq) -> 2 Al3+(aq) + 3 H2(g)

When total undissociated lactic and acetic acids exceed ~6 g/L (as lactic acid equivalents), multi-month storage trials (2 to 48 weeks at 20°C) reveal visible liner blistering in the can neck region (driven by hydrogen gas evolution) and dissolved aluminum leaching reaching up to 58 mg/L—nearly 100 times normal beer levels—which induces metallic astringency and protein-metal turbidity. Moreover, controlled 24-week trials across different polymer formulations show that certain acrylic liners (Acrylic-B) allow twice the aluminum dissolution (p < 0.05) of competing acrylic (Acrylic-A) and BPA-NI epoxy liners. Conducting multi-month polymer liner interaction and accelerated corrosion trials to prevent metal leaching and liner delamination in sour beers, ciders, or canned spirit cocktails is a textbook materials-science R&D activity under IRC § 41.
The Hard Science Foundation: Biochemistry, Microbiology, and Process Chemistry

To satisfy the "Technological in Nature" mandate of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4), a brewery or distillery's experimentation must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Every core stage of brewing and fermentation is governed by quantifiable biochemical and physical mechanisms.
Biochemical Pathways of Volatile Ester and Fusel Alcohol Synthesis

During fermentation, yeast absorbs wort sugars and amino acids, converting carbohydrates under anaerobic conditions into approximately equal concentrations of ethanol and carbon dioxide (CO2) while excreting hundreds of secondary metabolites—including esters, higher ("fusel") alcohols, carbonyls (aldehydes), vicinal diketones (diacetyl [2,3-butanedione] and 2,3-pentanedione, which yeast subsequently reduces to recycle excess NADH during warm maturation), and sulfur compounds (SO2 and H2S formed during methionine and cysteine transamination)—that define the sensory profile of beer, cider, and distilled spirit washes.

Ester formation requires two substrates: an acyl-CoA (principally Acetyl-CoA, the most plentiful acid intermediate produced by yeast) and an alcohol (either ethanol or a higher fusel alcohol). Peer-reviewed yeast metabolism literature (PMC6524682) shows that fusel alcohols—such as isoamyl alcohol, active amyl alcohol, and isobutanol—are synthesized either de novo from glycolytic pyruvate via the mitochondrial isoleucine-leucine-valine (ILV) pathway (catalyzed sequentially by acetolactate synthase [Ilv2], acetohydroxyacid reductoisomerase [Ilv5], dihydroxyacid dehydratase [Ilv3], and alpha-isopropylmalate synthase [Leu4/Leu9], which condenses alpha-ketoisovalerate with Acetyl-CoA subject to leucine and Zn2+-mediated CoA feedback inhibition) or through the degradation of branched-chain amino acids by Bat1 and Bat2.

The condensation of Acetyl-CoA with ethanol or higher alcohols is catalyzed intracellularly by the enzyme Alcohol Acyl-CoA Transferase (AAT, also termed Alcohol Acetyltransferase), whose production is governed by the transcription of the ATF1 gene. When AAT condenses Acetyl-CoA with ethanol, it yields ethyl acetate, which imparts a solvent-like (nail varnish remover), fruity, and sweet aroma; when AAT condenses Acetyl-CoA with isoamyl alcohol, it yields isoamyl acetate, which imparts a characteristic banana aroma. Minor esters formed from other higher alcohols (such as ethyl hexanoate [pineapple] and ethyl propionate [rum/grape]) combine synergistically even below their individual detection thresholds to create complex fruity profiles. Although fermentation is an anaerobic process, brewers introduce controlled doses of dissolved oxygen at the start of fermentation. Yeast prioritizes this initial oxygen to synthesize sterols and unsaturated fatty acids required for cell membrane synthesis and cell growth. Crucially, the presence of dissolved oxygen and unsaturated fatty acids directly inhibits the production of the AAT enzyme and reduces the expression of the ATF1 gene, suppressing ester synthesis whenever aerobic membrane synthesis is active.

Because desirable high levels of isoamyl acetate frequently co-occur with ethyl acetate production in high-sugar fermentations, brewers face acute technical uncertainty in balancing oxygenation, temperature, hydrostatic pressure, and wort FAN to hit target isoamyl acetate levels without crossing into solvent-like ethyl acetate defects.

In the laboratory, technical teams quantify these experimental outcomes using Headspace Gas Chromatography coupled with Flame Ionization and Flame Photometric Detection (HS-GC-FID-FPD) (utilizing a 30 m x 0.25 mm DB-WAXETR capillary column with 0.5 um layer thickness and a 129.8 ppm 2-heptanol internal standard to quantify 17 volatile aroma compounds, where ethyl acetate elutes at ~3.000 minutes), alongside gravimetric measurements of Apparent Degree of Attenuation (ADA) and Alcohol by Volume (ABV) derived from Original Extract (OE, in °P), Residual Extract (RE, in °P), Original Gravity (OG), and Final Gravity (FG):
ADA (%) = ((OE - RE) / OE) x 100
Microbiology, Pure Yeast Culture Isolation, and Competitive Acidification

Academic curricula in brewing science—spanning certificate, associate, bachelor's, master's, and doctoral programs—train specialists in advanced microbiology, biochemistry, and process engineering to manage yeast genetics, cultivation, and sanitation.

During active fermentation, brewer's yeast secures its ecological environment against microbial competitors through three simultaneous biochemical mechanisms: (1) consuming dissolved oxygen to establish an anaerobic environment, (2) generating toxic alcohol, and (3) excreting organic acids (via the Krebs/citric acid cycle pathway during essential amino acid synthesis) that rapidly drop the liquid pH from approximately 5.2 in the wort down to 4.0 in finished beer. When brewers or distillers trial novel yeast strains, stress-test yeast propagation under varying hydrostatic pressure in tall fermenters (which correlates with altered production of fusel alcohols and esters), or evaluate cell viability using a microscope, hemacytometer, and methylene blue or methylene violet staining (where viable cells enzymatically reduce the dye to a colorless product), they are conducting applied microbiological research.
Hop Isomerization Thermodynamics, Photolytic Cleavage (3-MBT), and Colloidal Stabilization

Hop cones contain resinous lupulin glands rich in hydrophobic alpha-acids (humulones; typically 10%–20% of dry weight in bittering hops and 2%–10% in aromatic hops), beta-acids (lupulones, <5%), polyphenols (3%–6% of total cone dry weight, including the hop-specific prenylflavonoid xanthohumol at 0.002–1.2 ppm in beer), and volatile essential oils (0.5%–3.0% of dry mass, comprising ~300 compounds led by myrcene [68%], alpha-humulene [13.3%], and beta-caryophyllene [3.7%]). During wort boiling, insoluble humulones undergo thermal acyloin ring contraction (isomerization) into water-soluble bitter iso-alpha-acids (cis- and trans-isohumulones, yielding 10–100 ppm in finished beer). To maximize hop oil and alpha-acid extraction while minimizing vegetative trub losses, breweries trial cryogenic separation products (Cryo Hops®, patented by Yakima Chief Hops in 2017), in which whole-leaf hops are flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen in a low-oxygen environment and passed through a single mechanical sieve to separate concentrated lupulin from leafy bract matter. According to Yakima Chief Hops technical reports, because cryogenic lupulin pellets hold roughly double the resin and oil concentration of standard T-90 pellets (dosed at 40%–50% of T-90 weight) and remove bract-borne enzymes responsible for "hop creep" refermentation, experimental brewing trials with cryo-separated hops reduce vegetal astringency and decrease wort/beer trub absorption—for example, allowing Wander Brewing to shrink total hop weight by 25% while increasing per-batch beer yield by ~6%.

Iso-alpha-acids are also highly susceptible to photochemical degradation. Exposure to ultraviolet light (UV-B, <380 nm) directly excites isohumulones into a singlet state, while blue visible light (350–500 nm, which penetrates clear glass and green glass above 400 nm) excites riboflavin into a triplet state that removes an electron from isohumulones. Both pathways trigger a Norrish Type 1 photolytic cleavage of the side chain at the acyloin group; the cleaved radical loses its carbonyl group and traps a sulfhydryl radical (derived from riboflavin-sensitized oxidation of the sulfur-containing amino acid cysteine) to form 3-methyl-2-butene-1-thiol (3-MBT). Because 3-MBT has a human sensory detection threshold of approximately 4 parts per trillion (ppt) (equivalent to 4 mL in 500 Olympic-sized swimming pools), breweries conduct R&D trials with catalytically hydrogenated/reduced iso-alpha-acid extracts—dihydro- (rho), tetrahydro- (tetra), and hexahydro-iso-alpha-acids—whose reduced side chains do not form flavor-active 3-MBT upon light exposure and simultaneously enhance beer foam stability and cling.

Downstream in the cellar, colloidal haze in beer (which peaks near pH 4.0) results from hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic pi-stacking between proline-rich haze-active (HA) barley hordein proteins (~20 mol% proline) and proanthocyanidin polyphenols (such as procyanidin B3 and prodelphinidin B3 dimers, of which 70%–80% originate from barley malt and 20%–30% from hops). At <=4°C, non-covalent complexes form reversible "chill haze" (which redissolves at 20°C); upon oxidation and acid catalysis over time, aided by trace iron (Fe) and copper (Cu) chelation, these complexes form irreversible covalent "permanent haze". To achieve shelf stability without stripping flavor or foam, brewers conduct systematic fining and filtration trials using silica hydrogels (such as Siligel) and silica xerogels—which selectively adsorb haze-forming proteins while leaving foam-stabilizing proteins intact—paired with PVPP (polyvinylpolypyrrolidone, a polyamide structurally mimicking polyproline that adsorbs flavanoid polyphenols at ~10 g/hL dosage), colloidal silica sols (Spindasol SB1), and beta-glucanase/hemicellulase enzymes. Engineers and QA chemists evaluate these trials by measuring nephelometric turbidity at EBC 90° and EBC 25° (alongside proteic stability under EBC Analytica 9.40 and 9.41), and by testing polymeric membrane filtration (lenticular modules and PES/PP cartridges) as a cold-stabilization alternative to thermal pasteurization.
Regulatory Framework: Applying the IRC § 41 Four-Part Test and QRE Rules

Claiming the federal R&D tax credit requires satisfying both the activity qualification standards of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d) (the Four-Part Test) and the strict expenditure eligibility rules of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2.
The Statutory Four-Part Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4)

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A), the Four-Part Test must be applied separately to each business component—defined in § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business. Importantly for breweries and distilleries, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C) establishes a Special Rule for Production Processes: any plant process, machinery, or technique for the commercial production of a beverage is treated as a separate business component distinct from the beverage being produced. Thus, even if a brewery is producing an established flagship lager, an experimental project to redesign the wort cooling loop, automate fermentation temperature control, or reduce canning line DO pickup is evaluated as its own standalone process business component.

headers: Qualifying Brewery / Distillery Application vs. Excluded Activity

cells: Research must be intended to develop a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of a business component. Research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors is statutorily disqualified under § 41(d)(3)(B).

Qualifies: Formulating a shelf-stable reduced-alcohol IPA, a gluten-free beer via enzymatic hydrolysis, a sour beer can liner protocol preventing Al3+ leaching, or a high-yield mash/distillation regime. Excluded: Tweaking hop bills purely for subjective consumer taste preference, seasonal branding, or aesthetic label design.

The process of experimentation used to discover information must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Existing scientific principles and technologies may be employed.

Qualifies: Applying biochemistry (ATF1/AAT enzyme kinetics, protease hydrolysis), microbiology (mixed-culture dynamics, cell viability), analytical chemistry (HS-GC-FID-FPD, EBC turbidity), or mechanical/chemical engineering (isobaric filling dynamics, heat transfer). Excluded: Market research, consumer focus panels, management efficiency surveys, or economic modeling (§ 41(d)(4)(D), (G)).

Expenditures must qualify under § 174A / § 174 as activities undertaken to eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design of developing or improving the component as of the project's outset. Does not require exceeding common industry knowledge or achieving a scientific breakthrough (Appeals of Walden; TD 9104), nor does the project need to succeed (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii)).

Qualifies: Resolving how to control wort DO2 and fermentation temperature in a new cylindroconical tank geometry to suppress ethyl acetate (<18 mg/L) while maintaining isoamyl acetate (>1.8 ppm), or how to prevent chill haze without pasteurization. Excluded: Scaling up an already proven recipe where the method and parameters are known, or routine production after commercial production begins (§ 41(d)(4)(A)).

Substantially all (80% or more) of the research activities for the business component (measured on a cost or reasonable basis) must constitute elements of a systematic process of evaluating alternatives (modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error involving hypothesis, testing, data analysis, and refinement per Siemer Milling Co., T.C. Memo. 2019-37, and Little Sandy Coal Co., 62 F.4th 287). If the whole component fails the 80% test, the shrinking-back rule (§ 1.41-4(b)(2)) applies the test to the most significant subset of elements.

Qualifies: Running sequential pilot brews or distillation runs with documented hypotheses, systematically varying mash pH, enzyme dosage, or nitrogen purge durations (e.g., 8s vs. 5s) and analyzing GC/HPLC, EBC turbidity, or DO meter results. Excluded: Unstructured "simple trial and error" (e.g., replacing machine bearings in Siemer Milling), ordinary construction fixes (Walden), or routine QC testing (§ 41(d)(4)(D)(v)).

body.text: Three judicial principles from recent litigation directly govern how breweries and distilleries must structure their claims:

items: Systematic vs. Simple Trial and Error (Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37): In Siemer Milling, the U.S. Tax Court disallowed $238,670 in R&D tax credits ($122,424 for 2011 and $116,246 for 2012) claimed by a wheat flour miller across seven projects (including flour heat-treatment, wheat hybrid testing, and ozone integration) because the taxpayer failed to demonstrate a scientific process of experimentation. The court held that a valid process of experimentation "must involve a methodical plan involving a series of trials to test a hypothesis, analyze the data, refine the hypothesis, and retest the hypothesis so that it constitutes experimentation in the scientific sense". Unstructured adjustments or simple trial-and-error tinkering on the production floor do not qualify. However, the Tax Court in Siemer Milling also rejected the IRS's argument that an R&D project cannot span multiple tax years, holding that there is no statutory requirement that a taxpayer face a different technical uncertainty each year so long as technical uncertainty exists in the claim year.

The 80% "Substantially All" Fraction and the Shrinking-Back Rule (Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, aff'd, 62 F.4th 287, 7th Cir. 2023): Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), the numerator of the 80% fraction consists of research activities constituting elements of a process of experimentation, and the denominator consists of all research activities for the business component deductible under § 174 / § 174A and not excluded under § 41(d)(4). In Little Sandy Coal, the Seventh Circuit affirmed the disallowance of credits where the taxpayer relied on arbitrary, unsubstantiated employee time estimates and an "all-or-nothing" claim at the whole-product level without documenting subcomponents under the shrinking-back rule (26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)). For a brewery or distillery, if an overall facility upgrade includes ordinary construction or routine equipment installation (which dilutes the process-of-experimentation ratio below 80%, as occurred in In the Matter of the Appeals of Walden), the tax specialist must apply the shrinking-back rule to isolate the specific experimental subcomponent—such as the custom inline DO sensor control loop or the experimental mash filter protocol.

Experimental Control Groups vs. Routine Data Collection and Cohan Estimation Limits (George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10): Recent 2026 Tax Court precedent in George v. Commissioner underscores that biological and agricultural formulation trials conducted with documented experimental protocols, recipe records, and control groups qualify under § 41, while warning taxpayers on the strict evidentiary limits of the Cohan rule for estimating undocumented R&D supply and wage allocations when routine production logs are retroactively recast as R&D studies after the fact.

body.text: Qualified Research Expenses (QREs), Statutory Exclusions, and Correction of the Expenditure Model

Once qualified research activities are established under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d), only specific expenditure categories enumerated in 26 U.S.C. § 41(b) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2 may be claimed as Qualified Research Expenses (QREs). Eligible in-house and contract research expenditures fall into four statutory categories:

First, In-House Employee Wages (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), § 41(b)(2)(D), § 3401(a); 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)–(d)) comprise federal taxable wages reported on Form W-2 (including bonuses and taxable stock option redemptions attributable to grant-year qualified services, but excluding non-taxable fringe benefits, 401(k) contributions, and pre-tax health insurance) paid for qualified services performed in the United States. Qualified services encompass three functional tiers: (a) engaging in qualified research (brewmasters, head distillers, fermentation scientists, microbiologists, food technologists, and process or packaging engineers formulating hypotheses, running pilot batches, or analyzing GC/HPLC data); (b) direct supervision (immediate first-line technical management of qualified research, excluding higher-level executives to whom first-line managers report); and (c) direct support (hands-on support directly tied to experimental runs—such as cellar workers cleaning and sterilizing pilot fermenters between trials, lab technicians preparing methylene blue slides or compiling experimental batch logs, and machinists fabricating prototype canning line manifolds, while excluding general administrative, payroll, accounting, or routine janitorial staff). Under the "Substantially All" rule for wages (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)), if at least 80% of an employee's wages during the taxable year are allocated to qualified services, 100% of that employee's W-2 wages for the year qualify as QREs.

Second, In-House Supplies (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), § 41(b)(2)(C); 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)) are defined as any tangible property other than land, improvements to land, and property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. In breweries, cideries, and distilleries, qualifying supplies include specialty hops, experimental malt bills, fruit batches, yeast cultures, enzymes, fining agents, laboratory reagents, trial aging barrels (when treated as non-depreciable consumables), and prototype cans, crowns, and polymer liners consumed or destroyed during experimental trials. Because 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) specifies that research need not succeed to qualify, raw materials consumed in failed or scrapped experimental batches are fully eligible supply QREs. However, if a trial batch is subsequently sold commercially as inventory, the taxpayer must ensure compliance with 26 U.S.C. § 263A uniform inventory capitalization rules (which IRC § 174A does not override) and properly allocate mixed-use raw materials between R&D and commercial production. Depreciable brewing equipment (fermenters, stills, canning lines) and equipment lease costs cannot be claimed as supply QREs.

Third, Computer Rental / Cloud Computing for R&D (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii); 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(4)) covers amounts paid to another person for the right to use off-premises, non-taxpayer-owned computers (such as cloud-based fermentation kinetics modeling, batch-yield sensor analytics, or shelf-life modeling platforms) in the conduct of qualified research.

Fourth, Contract Research Expenses (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A); 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)) are generally limited to 65% of amounts paid to third-party non-employees (such as external microbiology laboratories conducting HS-GC-FID-FPD or ELISA gluten assays, external fermentation consultants, or packaging engineering firms; rising to 75% for qualified research consortia under § 41(b)(3)(C) and 100% for eligible small businesses, universities, or federal laboratories performing qualified energy research under § 41(b)(3)(D)). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2)–(3), contract research qualifies only if a three-part test is met: (1) the agreement is entered into prior to performance of the research, (2) the research is performed on behalf of the taxpayer (the taxpayer retains substantial rights to the results, even if non-exclusive), and (3) the taxpayer bears the economic risk of failure (must pay even if the research fails; success-contingent fees are disqualified). Under § 41(b)(3)(B), prepaid contract research is creditable only in the tax year the research is actually conducted.
Statutory Correction of the HTML Dashboard ("Overheads/Utilities")

While the dashboard's inclusion of failed batches (raw materials consumed in scrapped experimental runs) is statutorily valid under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), its inclusion of "Overheads/Utilities" ($5,000 and $25,000) violates U.S. federal tax law under IRC § 41. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1)–(2) and the IRS Research Credit Audit Techniques Guide, expenditures for supplies or for the use of personal property that are indirect research expenditures or general and administrative expenses do not qualify as in-house research expenses. Specifically, the IRS Audit Techniques Guide states that overhead (facility leases, general factory overhead, licenses, administrative costs) and standard utility costs (electricity, water, steam, and natural gas used in facility operations) do not qualify as tangible property or supplies under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C). (Consumable utilities such as power and water used directly in R&D trials are routine qualifying expenditures in certain non-U.S. jurisdictions such as the United Kingdom and Australia, which explains their appearance in generic international templates, but they must be excluded from standard U.S. IRC § 41 claims.)

body.text: Worked Hypothetical Example: Recomputing the Brewery QRE Model under IRC § 41

items: Step 1 — Audit of the Unadjusted Figures: The unadjusted dollar increase is $135,000 - $55,000 = $80,000. Dividing $80,000 by the $55,000 baseline yields +145.45% (matching the dashboard's +145% label), and the generalist captures $55,000 / $135,000 = 40.74% (matching the doughnut chart's 40% Captured / 60% Missed). However, the ratio of $135,000 to $55,000 is 2.45x, not 3x as stated in the dashboard's narrative text.

Step 2 — Statutory Adjustment under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2): Disallowing the $5,000 and $25,000 Overheads/Standard Utilities line items yields U.S. IRC § 41-compliant QREs of $50,000 for the Generalist ($35,000 Supplies + $15,000 Wages) and $110,000 for the Specialist ($45,000 Supplies including 4 failed yeast propagation or sour beer liner pilot batches + $65,000 Wages capturing iterative fermentation and filtration trials on the brewery floor). The IRC § 41 uplift is ($110,000 - $50,000) / $50,000 = $60,000 / $50,000 = +120.00% uplift (a 2.20x multiple, where the generalist captures 45.45% of eligible QREs and misses 54.55%, or $60,000 in qualifying expenditures).

Step 3 — Federal R&D Tax Credit Calculation on Form 6765 (ASC Method and IRC § 280C Election): Taxpayers compute their federal credit on Form 6765 using either the Regular Credit (Section A)—which equals 20% of current-year QREs exceeding a base amount (with a start-up fixed-base percentage of 3% for the first 5 years and a statutory maximum fixed-base percentage of 16% under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(C))—or the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC, Section B). If the hypothetical brewery is in its fourth year of claims and beyond with an established prior 3-year average QRE of $80,000, the ASC base amount is 50% of that 3-year average ($80,000 x 0.50 = $40,000), and the gross credit is 14% of current-year QREs exceeding $40,000: the Generalist claim yields ($50,000 - $40,000) x 0.14 = $1,400, whereas the Specialist claim yields ($110,000 - $40,000) x 0.14 = $9,800 (a 7.00x increase in gross credit because the historical base amount is fixed). Finally, under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c) and Form 6765 Line 26 instructions, a taxpayer making the irrevocable § 280C reduced-credit election on its original timely filed return multiplies the gross credit by 79% (100% minus the 21% corporate tax rate) to retain 100% of its immediate domestic § 174A deduction, resulting in a net federal tax credit of $7,742.00 ($9,800 x 0.79) under the Specialist claim compared to $1,106.00 ($1,400 x 0.79) under the Generalist claim.

Academic grounding in hard sciences (biochemistry, microbiology, chemical/process engineering) combined with exclusive focus on IRC § 41 / § 174A legislation and IRS audit defense.
Generalists classify experimental production runs as routine COGS; specialists isolate the underlying scientific activities on the brewhouse, cellar, or stillhouse floor.
Evaluates commercial or financial outcomes; often confuses routine recipe changes with R&D or misses process engineering trials entirely.
Distinguishes disqualified taste/style tweaks (§ 41(d)(3)(B)) from genuine biochemical or engineering uncertainties (e.g., ATF1 repression, Al3+ can liner corrosion, or colloidal haze kinetics).
Prevents both underclaiming (missing floor-level yeast, filtration, and packaging trials) and overclaiming (including disqualified aesthetic or routine QC work).
Relies primarily on general ledger invoices, payroll registers, and high-level financial summaries.
Directly interprets HS-GC-FID-FPD ester chromatograms, Competitive ELISA gluten assays, EBC 90°/25° turbidity logs, DO/TPO meter logs, and hemacytometer viability counts.
Links empirical scientific measurements directly to the resolution of technical uncertainty, satisfying the Siemer Milling scientific method standard.
Tends to apply broad, arbitrary percentage estimates across whole departments or entire product lines.

Maps employee time, pilot batch supplies, and 65% contract research to discrete business components (or subcomponents via 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) shrinking-back) while excluding disallowed overheads under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2).
Protects the claim from summary disallowance under Little Sandy Coal (7th Cir. 2023) for failure to prove the 80% process-of-experimentation threshold.
Defends claims primarily by substantiating financial expenditure receipts rather than scientific methodology.

body.text: A generalist accountant examining a brewery's ledger sees line items for malted barley, hops, yeast cultures, silica gel filter aids, and aluminum cans, treating them uniformly as manufacturing inputs. A specialist trained in fermentation science recognizes when those same physical inputs were consumed in an iterative, hypothesis-driven experiment—such as testing four sequential yeast propagation pressure profiles to prevent fusel alcohol spikes, evaluating twelve boil temperature curves with cryo-separated lupulin to optimize alpha-acid isomerization, running silica xerogel and PVPP dosage matrices to eliminate chill haze at EBC 90°, or conducting 24-to-48-week sour beer storage trials across BPA-NI epoxy and acrylic can liners to stop aluminum leaching.
Contemporaneous Documentation, Form 6765 Section G, and Audit Resilience

The procedural landscape governing R&D tax credit claims has tightened substantially following federal court decisions in United States v. Harper (847 Fed. App'x 408, 9th Cir. 2021) and Premier Tech, Inc. v. United States (No. 2:20-cv-890, D. Utah July 15, 2022), alongside the Tax Court's evidentiary rulings in Siemer Milling (2019), Little Sandy Coal (2021/2023), and George v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2026-10). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d), a taxpayer claiming a credit under Section 41 must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit.
Upfront Disclosure on Amended Returns and Form 6765 Section G (2026 Mandate)
Breweries and distilleries must comply with two distinct tiers of upfront IRS reporting depending on whether the claim is filed on an original return or an amended return (refund claim).

First, for Research Credit Refund Claims on Amended Returns, Treasury Regulation § 301.6402-2(b)(1) requires that a refund claim set forth in detail each ground upon which a credit or refund is claimed and facts sufficient to apprise the Commissioner of the exact basis thereof. Under IRS requirements (IR-2021-203, effective January 10, 2022, as updated on June 18, 2024 in FAQ 21), taxpayers filing an amended return to claim an R&D credit refund must submit three mandatory elements upfront at the time of filing: (1) identification of all business components to which the Section 41 research credit claim relates for that year; (2) for each business component, a description of all research activities performed; and (3) the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year (which may be reported on Form 6765). Two previously required upfront elements—the names of individuals who performed each research activity and the information each individual sought to discover—were waived at the time of filing effective June 18, 2024, though the IRS retains the authority to request them during an audit.

Second, for Original and Amended Returns under Updated Form 6765 Section G, the final updated Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025, released February 6, 2026) establish that Section G (Business Component Information) was optional for tax years beginning before 2026 (unless filing an amended return) but becomes mandatory for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026. Under the "80%/Top 50" reporting rule, filers required to complete Section G must itemize their research projects by individual business component—classifying each in Column 49(d) as Product, Process, or All Others (formula, technique, invention, or software) and breaking down direct wages, supervision wages, support wages, supplies, computer rental, and contract research across Columns 50–56—covering a minimum of 80% of total QREs reported on Line 48, up to a maximum of 50 business components (with any remaining components reported in aggregate by entering "Aggregate Business Components" in Column 49(c)). A brewery, cidery, or distillery is exempt from completing Section G for tax years beginning after 2025 if it qualifies for one of two exceptions: (a) the Qualified Small Business (QSB) Payroll Tax Election under 26 U.S.C. § 41(h)(3) (a corporation or partnership with under $5 million in current-year gross receipts and no gross receipts for any tax year before the 5-tax-year period ending with the current tax year that checks the box on Form 6765 Line 33a to apply up to $500,000 of its research credit against employer Social Security payroll taxes in Section D via Form 8974); or (b) the Small-Filer Exception for taxpayers with controlled-group QREs on Line 48 of $1.5 million or less, average annual gross receipts of $50 million or less for the prior three tax years (determined under § 448(c)(3)), and a research credit claimed on an original return.
Actionable Protocol for Brewery and Distillery R&D Substantiation

To build an audit-resilient technical record that satisfies both the Siemer Milling scientific experimentation standard and Form 6765 Section G project accounting, brewery and distillery management should implement three operational controls:

items: Establish Project-Coded Scientific Batch and Lab Tracking: Assign a unique alphanumeric business-component identifier (matching Column 49(c) of Form 6765) to every experimental recipe, fermentation kinetics trial, distillation cut study, filtration test, or canning line engineering project prior to execution. Link all contemporaneous analytical data—HS-GC-FID-FPD volatile ester and congener chromatograms, Competitive ELISA gluten results, EBC 90° and EBC 25° nephelometric turbidity logs, hemacytometer yeast viability counts, mash/wort pH and gravity attenuation curves, and inline DO/TPO packaging logs—directly to that project code, explicitly recording failed or scrapped batches.

Document Hypotheses and Technical Uncertainties Contemporaneously: Before initiating pilot batches or equipment modifications, record a formal project brief defining the specific scientific or engineering uncertainty (capability, method, or design) and the testable hypothesis—for example, "Trialing three temperature-pressure profiles in a cylindroconical fermenter to determine whether restricting initial wort DO2 and holding controlled fermentation temperatures suppresses ATF1 gene expression sufficiently to keep ethyl acetate below 18 mg/L while maintaining isoamyl acetate above 1.8 ppm".

Integrate Technical Personnel with Specialized R&D Tax Advisors: Mandate structured review sessions between head brewers, master distillers, QA microbiologists, packaging engineers, and specialized biochemical R&D tax advisors. Ensure time-tracking records cleanly separate experimental hours (direct research, first-line supervision, and hands-on support) from routine commercial production, verify that third-party lab and engineering contracts satisfy the three-part risk-and-rights test under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e), and exclude non-qualifying general overheads and standard utilities under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2) prior to filing.
